groups.title: The Relational Model
groups.question: Explain the relational model in your own words and how it keeps data correct.

followUps.Tables, Keys & Relationships: What goes wrong when a table has no real primary key, or when foreign keys are only checked in application code?
followUps.Data Types & Schema Contracts: Why is storing a date in a text column a bad idea, even if every value looks right today?

evidence.text: Each row has a primary key that uniquely identifies it, so the same thing can't be stored twice.
A foreign key makes the database itself reject a row that points at something that doesn't exist.
Checks done only in application code can be bypassed by other code or by two requests at once, leaving orphan or duplicate rows.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (primary key, foreign key) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a foreign key is only a naming convention that the database doesn't enforce.

evidence.text: The database rejects values that don't fit a column's type, so invalid data can't get in.
Dates stored as text accept invalid or inconsistently formatted values and sort as strings, not as dates.
Queries then have to convert every value, which is slower and stops indexes from being used.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (VARCHAR, INT, data types) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says data types only matter for saving storage space.

groups.title: ACID & Transactions
groups.question: Walk through what a transaction is and what promises a database makes about it.

followUps.ACID Properties Explained: Two users buy the last ticket at the same moment. Which ACID property decides what happens, and how?
followUps.SQL vs NoSQL — When Each Fits: How would you decide between a relational and a document database for a new project?

evidence.text: All the steps of a transaction happen, or none do, so a half-done change never stays.
Transactions running at the same time don't see each other's unfinished work, which decides who gets the last ticket.
Once a transaction is committed, the change survives a crash.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (ACID, atomicity, isolation) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says atomicity means running on one thread, or that isolation gives each user their own copy of the database.

evidence.text: Relational databases enforce a schema, relationships and transactions, which fits connected data where correctness matters.
Document databases store self-contained, flexible records, which fits data read as a whole or with a changing shape, and they spread across machines easily.
The choice depends on how connected the data is and how it will be queried, trading off joins and consistency.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (SQL, NoSQL, MongoDB) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says NoSQL is always faster, or that SQL databases can't scale.

groups.title: Client/Server Architecture
groups.question: Explain what happens between your application sending a query and getting rows back.

followUps.How Databases Execute Queries: A query is slow. How does knowing the parse, plan and execute stages help you find where the time goes?
followUps.Connection Management: Why does opening a new database connection for every query break an app under load, and what fixes it?

evidence.text: A query is parsed, then planned (the planner picks how to fetch the rows), then executed.
Knowing the stages tells you whether time goes into a bad plan, the execution itself, or the network.
EXPLAIN shows the plan the planner chose, so you can see where a slow query spends its time.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (parser, planner, EXPLAIN) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a slow query is always a network problem.

evidence.text: Each connection costs the server memory and a process or socket, so there is a hard limit on how many it can hold.
Opening one per query under load uses up that limit, so new queries fail or wait.
A connection pool (in the app or PgBouncer/ProxySQL) reuses a small set of connections.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (connection, pool, PgBouncer) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says connections are free and the database can accept any number of them.

groups.title: Getting Started Practically
groups.question: Walk through how you would set up a local database and start working with it.

followUps.Installing & Connecting to PostgreSQL: You can't connect to a fresh PostgreSQL server. How does pg_hba.conf help you tell an auth problem from a network problem?
followUps.MySQL Workbench & Basic Administration: What do you lose if you only ever work through a GUI tool like MySQL Workbench?

evidence.text: pg_hba.conf decides which hosts, users and databases may connect and how they must authenticate.
An error naming pg_hba or authentication means the server was reached but rejected you; a timeout or refused connection is a network or listen problem.
You fix an auth rejection by adding or correcting a pg_hba.conf line and reloading, not by changing the network.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (psql, pg_hba.conf) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says pg_hba.conf is the network firewall that opens the port.

evidence.text: A GUI writes the SQL for you, so you don't learn what actually runs.
On a server where only a terminal is available, you can't work without knowing the SQL.
Use the GUI to visualise and inspect, and know the SQL underneath.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (MySQL Workbench, GUI) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says using a GUI teaches you the same as writing SQL yourself.
